strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: Theorems 1-2 uniquely characterize stable feature-learning parameterizations for PC as identical to BP's, constraining the design space meaningfully
Systematic framework using five desiderata that clearly derives constraints on scaling exponents through careful asymptotic analysis
Comprehensive experimental validation across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, CNNs, transformers) and datasets supporting theoretical predictions
Honest and thorough limitations discussion acknowledging gaps between linear theory and nonlinear practice, computational costs, and open questions
Provides theoretical justification for heuristic parameterizations in prior work, explaining why µP is the only scalable choice
Well-organized presentation with detailed appendix enabling reproducibility; code is made publicly available
weaknesses: Theory limited to linear networks while experiments only provide empirical evidence for nonlinearity; substantial gap between theoretical assumptions (exact equilibration) and practice (finite inference steps)

Main result—PC converges to BP under scalable parameterizations—provides no advantage over BP, and acknowledged instability of the fast saddle-to-saddle regime eliminates the primary proposed PC benefit

Practical applicability severely limited: requires ~100k inference steps per training step (making PC as slow as BP) and only 100 training steps shown (far from convergence); no final performance comparisons
Nonlinear experiments show brittleness: transformers required removal of layer normalization for convergence; missing error bars and limited architectural scope

Theory-practice gap insufficiently addressed: no analysis of finite-step inference dynamics, unclear what 'activity equilibrium seems to be reached' means operationally, no convergence rate characterization
N ≫ L regime is restrictive and impractical for realistic architectures; paper doesn't clarify minimum width-to-depth ratios needed or applicability to standard models like ResNet-50

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis deriving stable PC parameterizations through systematic verification of five desiderata; first principled framework for PC scaling with depth
Stronger results than prior work (Ishikawa et al. 2024): proves μP is the unique stable and feature-learning parameterization, not just showing existence
Comprehensive experimental validation: systematic width/depth sweeps, multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, ImageNet), modern architectures (CNNs, transformers), proper random seed averaging
Novel extension to depth-aware parameterizations with joint N,L→∞ limits and O(L/N) convergence rates for gradients; clean connection to recent BP theory extensions
Well-organized presentation with clear main results and practical implications; thorough appendix with detailed proofs; code made available for reproducibility
Identifies important practical issue: standard PyTorch parameterizations cause PC outputs to explode with width, providing actionable guidance
weaknesses: Core theoretical results (Theorems 1-2) restricted to linear networks; nonlinear validation is empirical rather than theoretical, limiting guarantees for practical architectures

Critical assumption of exact PC inference convergence (∂F/∂z*=0) not fully justified: experiments use finite iterations, convergence rates not analyzed, and Innocenti et al. (2025) reported deterioration of energy-loss correspondence during training
Restrictive L/N→0 requirement for depth results: standard architectures (Transformers, ResNets) have comparable L and N; results only meaningful for unusually wide-and-shallow networks

Limited practical impact: no demonstration that PC can train to convergence on real tasks; all large-scale experiments train for only 100 steps; computational cost of inference underexplored and potentially prohibitive
Heuristic extensions to practical settings: CNN/transformer parameterizations adapted from other work without theoretical justification; Adam learning rate scaling stated but not derived
Biological plausibility claims overstated: brain has comparable width and depth (doesn't satisfy L/N→0), and attention mechanisms are non-local, both violating key assumptions
